Issued at 154 PM EST Sun Nov 1 2026

Current advected layer PWAT imagery shows the deep sub tropical 
moisture plume flowing over the Desert SW, leading to widespread 
heavy rain and flooding there. At the same time, surface high 
pressure over the mid Atlantic is seeping south and beginning to 
surge lower level Gulf moisture northward into the central plains. 
In the upper levels, a long wave trough continues to deepen 
southward over the western US, which will amplify the pattern over 
the next several hours. Broad upper troughing exists over the 
central and eastern US with an embedded shortwave under the ridging, 
weakening as is continues east. Cloud cover will continue to move in 
this evening and tonight, which should limit fog development in most 
spots. Far southeast Chippewa county could see less cloud cover, 
resulting in a stronger surface inversion as warmer lake waters 
persist - leading to the best fog chances tonight. 

By Monday morning, the positive to neutrally tilted long wave 
troughing will reach the crest of the Rockies. A secondary piece of 
energy over the CAN/US border will keep this long wave troughing 
larger and curved. An upper jet streak rounding the base and 
extending into the central plains will work to enhance lee 
cyclogenesis over NE/SD. The secondary piece of upper energy will 
deepen and support this northern surface cyclone as it tracks 
towards MN Monday, while the long wave troughing still extends down 
to TX. Surface pressure falls will be seen on Monday over northern 
MI as the cyclone to the west deepens and reaches MN by late in the 
day. South winds will gradually become breezy by the late afternoon 
for northern MI, with mostly overcast skies. Temperatures will warm 
into the 60s, with the surface warm front lifting through the area 
Monday evening. Mild overnight temperatures will be seen as the rain 
shield associated with the cyclone approaches Lk MI's eastern 
shores. There is increasing confidence that deep moisture will be 
present in the central to northern plains, thanks to the sub 
tropical plume of mid to upper level moisture meeting the lower 
level Gulf moisture. PWATs of 1.3 to 1.7" are within the most likely 
solution space for this plume, which the HREF takes as far north as 
WI by late Monday. This evident WAA will bring a LLJ of 30 to 40kts 
around 2 to 4 kft over MI by early Tuesday. Gusty south to southwest 
winds will be seen over the coastal and coastal adjacent areas 
Tuesday. The initial surge of the warm, moist airmass just after 
midnight Tuesday will result in a surge of the precip shield over 
the U.P. and parts of NW lower. Aloft, upper ridging continues to 
exist over the L.P.. which results in mostly stable layers and 
little to no jet dynamics to increase precip chances farther south. 
After the initial surge of light to moderate rain Tuesday AM, a few 
different surface features will battle for the upper troughs focus 
and energy.. Most guidance favors this resulting in a slowly 
weakening cyclone over MN/WI for the remainder of Tuesday into early 
Wednesday. A break in rain, with warm temperatures, cloud cover and 
breezy south winds will be seen during the second half of Tuesday.

Here is where global models start to diverge. A certain group of 
ensembles generate a closed upper low over MN/IA by Wednesday 
morning, which would bring more favorable jet dynamics over norther 
MI for a return of light to moderate rain which would move over much 
of the area Wednesday (with shower chances into Thursday and Friday 
as it creeps over northern  MI and eastward). Another solution keeps 
it an open wave, which results in less forcing available and leads to 
less overall precipitation. There are even variations on how the 
closed low is deepening, with WPC clusters showing only a couple of 
percentages difference between the first 3 for Wednesday (day 4). 
This confirms higher variation with how global guidance is 
handling the larger scale forcing Wednesday and beyond. With all of 
this said, we have higher confidence in some things; first it will 
rain at least a little for most of northern MI (with NW lower and 
eastern upper seeing the most), temperatures will warm to near 
records Tuesday behind the warm front, anomalous moisture will move 
into the region late Monday and linger through mid week, and south 
winds will be gusty Tuesday. 

The uncertainty is in how much rain, will there be showers and storm 
potential, and when will this moist/warm airmass move out. With that 
said, we can also say for certain that we do not see a significant 
cool down in the forecast any time soon as mild Pacific air 
continues to flood the CONUS.
